title: A Safaitic memorial from Wādī al-Ḥašad dated by the year S¹ly fled from Rome — the only record in this corpus's Arabian holdings in which Rome is named in the text itself
language_note:
Safaitic, an Ancient North Arabian script and dialect of the basalt desert of southern Syria and north-eastern Jordan. `xna` here is the code the corpus already uses for arabia-03-jsnab17, and UNLIKE THERE IT IS THE RIGHT ONE: Safaitic is Ancient North Arabian, where JSNab 17 is Nabataean Aramaic. See arabia-05-ruwafa's language_note, which records that disagreement rather than resolving it.

THE EDITION PRINTS TRANSLITERATION ONLY — there is no Safaitic-script text in the article, so `original_text_excerpt` is a Latin-script rendering and not the script the stone carries. THREE NOTATIONS CARRY THE EDITORS' CONFIDENCE AND ALL THREE ARE PRESERVED BELOW: superscript ¹ distinguishes the Ancient North Arabian sibilants (s¹, and the corpus should expect s² and s³ elsewhere); square brackets mark a RESTORED letter, as in s¹l[y]; and braces mark letters read with UNCERTAINTY, as in ḫr{ṣ} and the whole closing invocation. The braces are not a bracket convention this project invented and they are not stripped: the closing eleven words of this text are almost entirely uncertain and an excerpt that dropped the braces would present them as read.
date: c. 12–9 BC, on the hunt's dating, tied to Syllaeus the Nabataean minister's stay at and departure from Rome under Augustus. THE RECORD DOES NOT DERIVE THIS AND DID NOT READ IT AT SOURCE. The article's historical section — which its own commentary points to as "the historical record (see below)" — was not among the pages captured, so the date is carried from F5_CANDIDATES.md and is the weakest-provenanced field in this record. A session with the PDF open should replace this with the editors' own statement and their argument for it.
original_text_excerpt: l tm bn ms¹k bn qtl bn brd bn ḥmt bn ġlmt bn mr bn ʾfty bn gml w wgm ʿl- ġyr w ʿlmlṭ w ʿl- qtl s¹nt ngy s¹l[y] mn rm w ḫr{ṣ} h- s¹nt f h bʿls¹mn ġw{ṯ} {w} {s¹}{l}{m} {w} {q}{b}{l}{l} {l}- {ḏ} {ʾ}{ḥ}{b}
original_text_note:
Verbatim from Al-Rawabdeh & Abbadi, Acta Orientalia Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae 70/1 (2017), PASTED BY THE CURATOR on 2026-09-05 from the REAL repository PDF. This session did not open the article.

EDITORIAL ACTS, DECLARED. None. The transliteration is reproduced exactly as pasted, including the closing invocation's braces, the single restored letter in square brackets, and the spacing of the ʿl- prefixes. No line division was printed in what was captured and none is supplied.

THE ONE ANOMALY, RECORDED AND NOT REPAIRED, AND IT IS ON A DEAD MAN'S NAME. The transliteration mourns three men — `ʿl- ġyr`, `ʿlmlṭ`, `ʿl- qtl` — and the translation renders them Ġyr, Mṭl and Qtl. TWO THINGS ARE OFF ON THE MIDDLE ONE AND ONLY ON THE MIDDLE ONE. Its consonants are m-l-ṭ in the transliteration and m-ṭ-l in the English, the same three letters transposed; and its ʿl- prefix is run together with the name where the other two are separated by a hyphen and a space. Two irregularities on one word is more likely the edition than the capture, and THIS RECORD DOES NOT DECIDE WHICH: both forms stand as printed, in the excerpt and in the translation, and a collation against the article's own plate or against OCIANA would settle it. The same restraint eastasia-05-liangshu-qin-lun exercised over 黝歙 and eastasia-07-tang-huiyao over 大定 — FINDING 55, a third time, and the first time on a Latin-script transliteration.

WHAT DID NOT GO WRONG, MEASURED BEFORE THE RECORD WAS WRITTEN. Square brackets balance 1:1 and braces balance 16:16 in the transliteration and 2:2 and 10:10 in the translation; every diacritic is a precomposed NFC character (ḥ ḫ ṣ ṭ ṯ ḏ ġ); the sibilant marker is U+00B9 SUPERSCRIPT ONE consistently in both fields, not a digit and not a modifier letter; and ʿ and ʾ are U+02BF and U+02BE, the half-ring modifier letters, not apostrophes. ONE ARTEFACT IS LEFT IN: the English ends with an unpaired U+201D right double quotation mark, which is the article's own quotation punctuation caught by the paste. It is not removed, because removing it would be a silent repair of the only evidence that the field was captured from a running page rather than retyped.
reference_translation:
By Tm son of Ms¹k son of Qtl son of Brd son of Ḥmt son of Ġlmt son of Mr son of ʾfty son of Gml and he grieved for Ġyr and for Mṭl and for Qtl the year {S¹ly} fled from Rm and {he kept watching} this year and so O Bʿls¹mn [grant] {help} {and} {security} {and} [show] {benevolence} {for} {whoever} {ʾḥb}”.

THE READING OF THE DATING FORMULA IS DISPUTED BETWEEN NAMED SCHOLARS, AND THE CLAUSE IN DISPUTE IS THE ONE THAT LINKS THIS TEXT TO ROME. The whole of the editors' discussion is given verbatim below, from the page the curator read; the inline footnote numeral after "the verb ḥwb" is removed and nothing else is altered.

"At the end of the inscription, the author asks the deity Bʿls¹mn to accept his prayer, and apparently he also asks for the prayers of other people to be accepted. This is dependent on the interpretation of the verb ʾḥb. Macdonald has translated the verb ʾḥb as “who has pursued a sinful course” when dealing with the inscription AbNSJ 1; this interpretation comes from the IV-form of the verb ḥwb. The verb ngy is attested in many Safaitic inscriptions, with the formula s¹nt ngy occurring more than forty times, and appears to have different meanings in many cases. Three particular meanings should be highlighted, which we shall list here. The first is the meaning attested in WH 1698, s¹nt ngy qṣr h- mdnt “the year Caesar announced the province”. Macdonald has interpreted this verb, and has suggested that the formula s¹nt ngy PN hdy should be understood as “in the year that PN was announced leader”, which he thinks makes reference to the conscripting of nomads into either the Roman or the Nabataean army. The interpretation is based on the word hdy, “leader”, since the interpretation of “escape” as we have understood it to mean in this inscription does not make a great deal of sense with reference to a leader (Macdonald 2014, pp. 154–155). A second meaning is the one found in HCH 102.1, s¹nt ngy rbbʾl “the year Rbbʾl escaped”. The third meaning is found in LP 424: s¹nt ngy mlk s¹lṭn “the year that Mlk retained power”. The verb retains the y in the feminine form as well, as evidenced by SIJ 786 which reads ngyt ʾ- mlkt “the Queen was announced”. Based on the similarity between this inscription and AbNSJ 1, in which the verb ngy is replaced with ‘ty, it seems likely that the meaning referred to here is the meaning “to escape”. This is corroborated by the historical record (see below) for it is known that Syllaeus left Rome and returned to the area where the inscription was found."

WHAT IS UNCERTAIN, AND IT IS NOT A SINGLE LETTER. The verb ngy carries at least three published senses in the Safaitic corpus, each attested and each cited: "announced" at WH 1698, s¹nt ngy qṣr h- mdnt, "the year Caesar announced the province"; "escaped" at HCH 102.1; and "retained power" at LP 424. MACDONALD READS THE FORMULA ONE WAY AND THESE EDITORS READ IT THE OTHER. On their reading this inscription is dated by a flight from Rome; on the sense Macdonald argues for elsewhere, s¹nt ngy PN would be a year in which someone was ANNOUNCED, and the editors say in their own words only that "it seems likely that the meaning referred to here is the meaning 'to escape'". Their argument is an analogy — AbNSJ 1, where ngy is replaced with ʿty — and a historical corroboration, not a demonstration from this stone.

AND THE CLOSING INVOCATION IS UNCERTAIN TWICE OVER. Its letters are braced throughout, meaning read with uncertainty; and its last word ʾḥb is separately disputed, the editors leaving it untranslated while recording that Macdonald renders the same verb at AbNSJ 1 as "who has pursued a sinful course", from the IV-form of ḥwb. The record carries the untranslated form the edition prints.

A NOTE ON WHAT IS *NOT* THE HEDGE HERE. F5_CANDIDATES.md proposed this record's gloss as the editors' remark that "the letter y has been added because it does not exist in the inscription" — the restoration in s¹l[y]. That sentence was not on the pages the curator read and is not quoted here. It is also the weaker hedge: it qualifies one letter of a name, where the ngy dispute qualifies what the sentence containing that name MEANS. The restoration itself is not lost — it is visible in the notation, s¹l[y] in the excerpt and {S¹ly} in the translation above.
translation_source:
Nada Al-Rawabdeh & Sabri Abbadi, "The Nabataean Minister Syllaeus in a New Ancient North Arabian (Safaitic) Inscription", Acta Orientalia Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae 70/1 (2017), 21–30. DOI 10.1556/062.2017.70.1.2. The English is the editors' own, printed with the transliteration and the commentary in the same article.

THE CITATION TRAP, RECORDED SO NOBODY RESOLVES IT THE WRONG WAY. The same two authors published a near-identical paper in Mediterranean Archaeology and Archaeometry 16/2 (2016), 33–40. This record cites the Acta Orientalia version and no claim here rests on the other.

findspot: Wādī al-Ḥašad, about 45 km north-east of the village of as-Ṣafawī, formerly known as H4, Jordan
notes:
F5 Part 3, record 38, and the second of the tranche's two Arabia verbatim_with_provenance slots.

ROME IS NAMED IN THE TEXT, AND NO OTHER ARABIAN RECORD IN THIS CORPUS CAN SAY SO. `rm` stands in the dating formula itself. The seed manifest flagged arabia-04-jabal-dabub in its own follow-up list as "not directly Rome-linked" and recommended supplementing it; arabia-01 and arabia-02 are a Greek periplus and a Palmyrene tariff, and arabia-03 is a tomb inscription. This is the region's first text in a local language that says the word.

WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT ROME, AND THE ANGLE IS THE POINT. It is not an embassy, a treaty or a trade notice. A man in the basalt desert records his ancestry for nine generations, grieves for three dead, asks Bʿls¹mn for help and security, and dates the whole of it by a piece of news from the imperial capital — the year Syllaeus fled from Rome. ROME APPEARS HERE AS A CALENDAR. That is a different kind of evidence from anything else in this corpus's Arabian holdings: not contact, but the reach of Roman political news into a nomadic community's sense of time. The man who guided Aelius Gallus's expedition into Arabia and was tried at Rome is, to this writer, simply what happened the year his friends died.

GLOSS-CAPABLE, contested_reading, AND THE DISPUTE FALLS ON THE ROME CLAUSE ITSELF. Macdonald against the editors on what s¹nt ngy means, with three published senses each attested at a named siglum, and the editors' own "it seems likely". This is stronger than the hedge F5_CANDIDATES proposed and the record says why in reference_translation. THE MECHANICAL REQUIREMENT IS MET: the dispute and the statement of uncertainty both sit inside reference_translation, which the loader chunks, and neither is in notes, which it does not.

THE DURABILITY WEAKNESS, WHICH IS REAL AND WHICH arabia-04 DOES NOT CARRY. THE INSCRIPTION HAS NO CORPUS SIGLUM. The article calls it "Inscription 1", so this record is addressable only through the article — where the same commentary cites WH 1698, HCH 102.1, LP 424, SIJ 786 and AbNSJ 1, five texts that DO have sigla, in its own argument. If the inscription is later published into OCIANA or another corpus it will acquire a number this record does not have, and the two will be hard to join. Recorded rather than solved.

THE BOUNDARY, STATED. What was captured is the transliteration, the translation, one paragraph of commentary and the findspot sentence. NOT CAPTURED AND NOT STOOD BEHIND: the article's historical section on Syllaeus — which is where its date comes from and therefore where this record's `date` field ultimately comes from, at one remove through a hunt document; its plates; and Macdonald 2014, pp. 154-155, which is quoted here only as the editors report it. The corpus has Macdonald's position at one remove and does not stand behind the editors' characterisation of it.

AND ONE THING THIS RECORD IS THE OCCASION OF RATHER THAN THE SUBJECT OF. Its licence turned out not to be a licence, and checking it revealed that two of the tranche's other three remaining captures have no stated terms at all. FINDING 69 names the vocabulary defect and ruling 74 sets the standard; this record is the first written under it.

The pinned 2026-08-10 Pleiades snapshot was searched for hasad, hašad, safawi, ṣafaw and ḥarra and returns nothing for any of them; the only near hits are two places titled Namara, at 33.02/36.03 and 32.84/36.65, which are a different site and are refused. GEONAMES WAS NOT SEARCHED — it needs the JO country file passed to `--geonames-find` on the host, which this session had no shell to run, and PLACES.md requires a GeoNames note to say what its coordinate denotes. THE ARTICLE PRINTS A LOCATION MAP (its Figure 1, a Google Earth capture with a pin between as-Ṣafawī and a label reading wādī al-Ḥašad) AND NO COORDINATES ARE TAKEN FROM IT. Reading a latitude off a satellite screenshot is authoring a coordinate, which is the one thing this schema exists to prevent; what the record fixes is the region and the bearing and distance the editors state.

subject_places.name: Rome (rm)
subject_places.note:
`stated` because the text names it: `rm`, in the dating formula `s¹nt ngy s¹l[y] mn rm`. ID CONFIRMED AGAINST THE PINNED SNAPSHOT AND THE METHOD IS RECORDED BECAUSE IT NEARLY WENT WRONG. Pleiades 423025 Roma appears in data/pleiades-names-20260810.csv.gz on four name-rows, ALL FOUR carrying an empty coordinate, an empty extent and locationPrecision `unlocated` — which would have made this a case for the `unlocated` key. It is not. The PLACES dump, data/pleiades-places-20260810.csv.gz, gives 423025 a representative point at 41.8899769865 / 12.4912581746, a real polygon extent, locationPrecision `related` and feature types `urban, settlement`. THE NAMES DUMP IS NOT WHERE COORDINATES LIVE, and a placement resolved against it alone would have asserted `unlocated: true` about the best-located city in the gazetteer. PLACES.md tells the curator to use `--find`, which reads both; this session had no shell and read the two files directly instead.

IT IS NOT YET IN data/gazetteer.json's CACHE — searched, absent — SO `--check` WILL REPORT IT RED UNTIL A REFRESH IS RUN AGAINST THE PINNED DUMP. That is the same repair `africa-04-silko-talmis` needs for pleiades:786108, which F5 Part 2 diagnosed as resolvable-but-never-cached, and the two can be fixed in one run. It is NOT the eastasia-04 problem, where the id is absent from the pinned snapshot altogether.

`mentioned`, AND THE RESTRAINT IS DELIBERATE. Syllaeus moves out of Rome, which looks like a `source` edge — but a directional role requires a `focus`, and the place he moves TO is not named in this text. Assigning one would draw an edge with one end missing, which is exactly why eastasia-07-tang-huiyao placed Tokharistan as `mentioned`. PLACES.md is explicit that a block of nothing but `mentioned` needs no focus and must not be made to invent one, and this block is that case: Rome is the only place the text names, and the passage is organised around the writer's dead, not around Rome.
